videos.script: The same eight hundred thousand sales take seventy-nine megabytes in PostgreSQL and under ten in DuckDB. Same rows, same values. {{sizes}} The difference is the direction the bytes are written in. PostgreSQL writes a row, then the next row. DuckDB writes a column, then the next column. {{direction}} That one decision changes two things. A query that needs one column reads one column, and not the other ten that sit beside it. {{read}} And a column is easy to compress, because it holds one kind of value: seven shop keys repeated, small integers in a narrow range, the same department name thousands of times. {{compress}} Ana takes the file apart. Which encoding each column got, how much the order of the rows matters, and how a reader skips most of a file using the minimum and maximum written beside every block. {{apart}} And then the price. A column store is bad at the till's job: writing one row at a time. That is why lesson 1 kept two databases. {{price}}
